stops.name: Mecca, the house of Abu Bakr, her birth
stops.campa: In the quarter of the Banu Taym, in the house of Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, a daughter is born to Umm Ruman: Aishah, fourth child of the man who will be first of all men to believe. Islam is young, four years old, still a whispered thing among a handful of households. She is born already inside it, cradled by parents who have already staked everything on the Messenger's word, in a city that has not yet decided whether to kill him for it.

stops.name: Mecca, a childhood among the persecuted few
stops.campa: She grows up in a household under siege for its faith: her father beaten and nearly killed for preaching openly in the Kaaba precinct, his fortune spent buying the freedom of tortured slaves like Bilal. She hears, before she can well understand them, the names that will fill her later life — Khadija, Ali, Zayd, the secret prayers in the ravines. The Quraysh mock her father as a man led astray; she is raised knowing her family's whole worth is staked on one unseen God.

stops.name: Mecca, the dream of the silk and the betrothal
stops.campa: In the Year of Sorrow, with Khadija gone, Khawla bint Hakim urges the Messenger to marry again, and names the little daughter of his truest friend. He tells her afterward of a sign that had already answered him: an angel showing him, twice, a form wrapped in silk, saying, this is your wife. Aishah is a small child at play with her toys when the betrothal is settled over her head, sealed with a bride-gift, years still to pass before any wedding.
stops.quote: You have been shown to me twice in my dream. I saw you pictured on a piece of silk and some-one said, 'This is your wife.' When I uncovered the picture, I saw that it was yours. I said, 'If this is from Allah, it will be done.'

stops.name: Mecca, her father's flight and her sister's two belts
stops.campa: The night the assassins ring the Messenger's house, Abu Bakr slips away with him toward the cave of Thawr, leaving his household to fend for the household's danger alone. Aishah's elder sister Asma tears her own waist-belt in two, keeping one half for herself and using the other to tie the mouth of the food-sack sent after them into hiding — earning the name Dhat al-Nitaqayn, She of the Two Belts. Aishah, not yet eight, watches her family scatter into the plot of history.

stops.name: The desert road, her own emigration to Medina
stops.campa: Months after her father and the Messenger have gone, Zayd ibn Haritha and Abu Rafi come back to Mecca to fetch the households left behind. Umm Ruman, Aishah, and Fatimah bint Muhammad set out by camel-litter across the same stony road the Prophet took in secret. On the way Aishah's camel bolts and nearly overturns her litter; Zayd runs it down and steadies it, and the frightened company presses on, a child riding out of the city of her birth toward a city she has never seen.

stops.name: Medina, arrival and the reunited household
stops.campa: The little caravan reaches Medina and Aishah is delivered into her father's house, reunited with Abu Bakr in the city that has taken him in. She falls ill for a time with the fever that grips new arrivals from Mecca's dry air meeting Medina's damp palm-groves; her hair falls out and grows back thicker. She grows up now beside the mosque the Messenger has raised, a betrothed child in the household of the man closest to him, waiting the years out until the wedding the town already expects.

stops.name: Medina, the wedding feast of milk
stops.campa: In Shawwal of the first year of the Hijra the wedding is held. Aishah is playing on a swing with other girls when her mother comes for her, straightens her hair, and dresses her; she is brought weeping a little to the Messenger's house, and finds it filled with nothing grander than a bowl of milk passed from hand to hand among the guests — no feast of meat, no music but the plain gladness of the small community. She moves into a mud-brick room built against the mosque wall.
stops.quote: There was nothing in our wedding but a bowl of milk that was passed round among us.
stops.quote_source: Narrated by Aishah, cited in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra

stops.name: Medina, her chamber, revelation on her breast
stops.campa: Of all his houses the Messenger loves hers best, and it is often in her small room, her head against his chest or his against her lap, that the Quran continues to come down. She will say the revelation descended on him once while she lay beside him under one blanket during her courses, so that later ages know a wife's touch does not bar the Word. In her narrow room, palm-thatched and curtained, the heaviest verses of the young faith are received in the plainest of settings.
stops.quote: The Prophet used to lean on my lap and recite Qur'an while I was in menses.

stops.name: Medina, the broken bowl, a wife's jealousy forgiven
stops.campa: Among the Messenger's wives Aishah alone was never before married, and her jealousy of the others, living and dead, is famous and unhidden. When a dish of food arrives as a gift from another wife's house, Aishah strikes it from the servant's hands in a fit of temper and it shatters on the floor. The Messenger only gathers up the spilled food onto a whole plate sent back in exchange, and says of the household's youngest, most beloved wife: your mother is jealous; eat.

stops.name: Mount Uhud, carrying water to the wounded
stops.campa: Eleven years old and two years married, she is still light enough to run behind the ranks; when the archers break and the battle turns against the faithful below the mountain, Aishah and Umm Sulaym go back and forth to the wells with water-skins on their backs, filling them, emptying them into the mouths of the wounded, running out again. She sees the Messenger's own blood on his face, the broken tooth, the ring-marks driven into his cheek, and carries water to him among the rest.
stops.quote: On the day of Uhud, when some people retreated and left the Prophet, I saw Aishah bint Abu Bakr and Umm Sulaim, with their robes tucked up so that the bangles around their ankles were visible, carrying the water skins on their backs, then pouring the water in the mouths of the people, and returning to fill the water skins again.
stops.quote_source: Sahih al-Bukhari 2880 (narrated by Anas ibn Malik)

stops.name: Medina, the Battle of the Trench, hunger in her house
stops.campa: Ten thousand ring the city, and for weeks the community is held at the ditch the believers dug in a single frantic effort. In the small houses by the mosque the wives wait out the siege on short rations, hearing the digging, the war-cries, the wind rising at last that scatters the confederate host unfought. Aishah, a girl of the besieged town rather than of the field, learns in her own chamber what it is to sit inside a city that does not know if it will still stand by morning.

stops.name: The road out of Medina, the two races
stops.campa: On a journey together, still slight and quick on her feet, she challenges the Messenger to a foot-race and outruns him. Years later, grown fuller-bodied, she races him again on another journey and this time he wins, laughing: this is for that one. It is a small thing set beside battles and revelations, and she keeps it anyway among her memories of him — proof that the man the world calls Messenger also ran races with his wife on the open road and let her win once.
stops.quote: I had a race with him and I outstripped him on my feet. When I became fleshy, I had a race with him and he outstripped me. He said: This is for that outstripping.
